children: Over eighteen turbulent years, Elon Musk transformed Tesla
from a niche garage venture re-engineering sports cars into an industry-shattering titan preparing to literally launch vehicles into the air.

The trajectory started in 2008 with the original Roadster, a hand-assembled proof-of-concept built on a Lotus Elise glider that nearly bankrupted the startup before proving battery power could outperform internal combustion.

That high-cost experiment generated the capital and credibility needed to design the Model S in 2012 and the falcon-winged Model X in 2015, effectively redefining modern luxury vehicles as software-driven supercomputers on wheels.
Musk’s mainstream takeover followed with the mass-market Model 3 sedan in 2017 and the Model Y crossover in 2020.

Recent years have marked a pivot toward radical geometry and autonomy. The angular, stainless-steel Cybertruck arrived in 2023 as an uncompromising break from traditional utility design, followed by the steering-wheel-free Cybercab, cementing Tesla's
bet on automated mobility networks over traditional driver ownership.
The fleet’s evolution now circles back to its origins with the second-generation Roadster, which features thrusters designed to enable short flights. Tesla
testing facility in McGregor, Texas, on Thursday night, with Musk saying the next-gen model is the result of a cutting-edge electric vehicle manufacturer working with a leading rocket engine maker.

title: Batteries to thrusters: Tesla's 18-year road to the flying car
